## The navigation problem

::: {style="text-align: center; font-size: 1.2em;"}
"Knowing the **position** with respect to some **reference frame**"
:::

- Early navigators used **celestial navigation** to determine both their position and **time** on Earth.

- The navigation problem is also a **timekeeping problem**
  - The better the clock the better the position estimation.
  - Improvement of **atomic clocks** has enabled the development of **GNSS**.
  - Example: computation of longitude requires comparing the local time with a reference time.

## Coordinate frames

### Coordinate frames: ECEF


::: {.columns}

::: {.column}
- Coordinates describe the position of a point in space with respect to a **reference frame**.
- A reference frame is defined by:
  - An **origin** (point in space)
  - A set of **axes** (directions in space)
- \acr{ECEF} reference frame definition:
  - $z$ axis: points to the \acr{CTP}
  - $x$ axis: points to the intersection of the equator and the Greenwich meridian
  - $y$ axis: completes the right-handed system
:::

::: {.column}
![](assets/figures/frame_ecef.svg)
:::

:::

### Coordinate frames: WGS84


::: {.columns}

::: {.column}
- \acr{ECEF} (*Cartesian*) coordinates are not very intuitive for humans
- \acr{WGS84} uses longitude, latitude and height (i.e. *geodetic* coordinates)
- Example:
  - ECEF: $(4780698.293, 176319.056, 4204205.524)$
  - Geodetic (WGS84): $$(41.5003999^\circ, 2.1121937^\circ, 0.0)$$

:::

::: {.column}
![](assets/figures/frame_wgs84.svg)
:::

:::

### Coordinate frames: ENU


::: {.columns}

::: {.column}
- \acr{ENU} is a **local reference frame**
  - The \acr{ENU} frame is different for each point on the Earth surface!
- The \acr{ENU} frame is defined by:
  - $x$ axis: points to the East
  - $y$ axis: points to the North
  - $z$ axis: points to the zenith
- Used to describe e.g. errors in an intuitive way (e.g. horizontal and vertical errors)
:::

::: {.column}
![](assets/figures/frame_enu.svg)
:::

:::


## Positioning techniques

Determination of position follows this sequence:

::: {.incremental}
1. **Elecromagnetic signals** are received
2. These are processed to obtain **measurements** (observables): pseudorange, carrier phase, Doppler, ...
3. From measurements we compute **distances** relative to **reference points** or **nodes** (e.g. satellites)
4. From distances we compute the **position** of the receiver in a reference frame.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Multiple positioning techniques exist, depending on the type of measurements
:::

### Triangulation


::: {.columns}

::: {.column}
- \acr{AoA} technique
- Receiver *measures* **angles** between the receiver and the *nodes*
- The **intersection** of the lines of sight gives the position of the receiver.
- Only 2 nodes are needed to determine the position in 2D
:::

::: {.column}
![](assets/figures/aoa.svg)
:::

:::


### Hyperbolic trilateration


::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

- \acr{TDoA} technique
- Receiver measures the time difference between the propagation times of the signals coming from two sources
- The **intersection** of the hyperbolas gives the position of the receiver.
- Only 2 hyperbolas are needed to determine the position in 2D (but 3 nodes are needed to compute the hyperbolas)
- This is the technique used in e.g. \acr{LORAN}
:::

::: {.column}


![](assets/figures/tdoa.svg)

:::

:::

### Hyperbolic trilateration: equations

- Being
  - $(x_u, y_u)$ the 2D position of the user (unkown to be solved)
  - $(x_i, y_i)$ the 2D position of the $i$-th node (known positions)
  - $\Delta \tau_{ij}$ the time difference of arrival between nodes $i$ and $j$ (measurement)
- The navigation equation to be solved is
$$
\begin{aligned}
\Delta \tau_{21} = R_2 - R_1 &= \sqrt{(\color{red}{x_u} - x_2)^2 + (\color{red}{y_u} - y_2)^2} - \sqrt{(\color{red}{x_u} - x_1)^2 + (\color{red}{y_u} - y_1)^2} \\
\Delta \tau_{31} = R_3 - R_1 &= \sqrt{(\color{red}{x_u} - x_3)^2 + (\color{red}{y_u} - y_3)^2} - \sqrt{(\color{red}{x_u} - x_1)^2 + (\color{red}{y_u} - y_1)^2}
\end{aligned}
$$

### Range-based trilateration


::: {.column}

- \acr{ToA} technique
- Receiver measures the propagation times of the signals coming from a node
- The **intersection** of the circles/spheres gives the position of the receiver.
- Three circles are needed to determine the position in 2D (Four nodes are needed to determine the position in 3D)
- This is the technique used in e.g. \acr{GNSS}
:::

::: {.column}
![](assets/figures/toa.svg)
:::

### Range-based trilateration: measurements

Range measurements can be obtained through two different techniques:

- \acr{RTT}: propagation time to the node and back to the receiver is measured.
  - synchornization requirements are relaxed (clock errors are cancelled out)
  - *privacy* concerns, the node (system) *sees* the receiver
- One way
  - Users/Receivers only receive signals from the nodes (system)
  - receivers and nodes **must** be synchronized

## Observables

### GNSS uses ranges

- Basic range [measurement]{style="color:blue;"} model for the $i$-th satellite, including the [unknowns]{style="color:red;"} and the [known information]{style="color:green;"}:

$$
\color{blue}{PR_i} = \underbrace{\sqrt{(\color{red}{x_u} - \color{green}{x_i})^2 + (\color{red}{y_u} - \color{green}{y_i})^2 + (\color{red}{z_u} - \color{green}{z_i})^2}}_{geometric\ range} + \underbrace{c \cdot \color{red}{\delta t_u}}_{clock\ error} + \underbrace{\varepsilon_i}_{noise}
$$

- Mathematically, the resulting system results in a set of **quadratic equations**

### Travel time (unbiased)

![](assets/figures/code_transmission.svg)

### Travel time (sat biased)


![](assets/figures/code_transmission_biased_sat.svg)

### Travel time (sat + rx biased)


![](assets/figures/code_transmission_biased_sat_rx.svg)

### Travel time computation

- Transmit time: $\tau = t_{u} - t_{i}$
- Pseudo travel time (with biases): $\tilde{\tau} = \tau + \color{red}{\delta t_{u}} - \color{green}{\delta t_{i}}$
- Pseudorange: $\color{blue}{PR} = c \cdot \tilde{\tau} = c \cdot (\tau + \color{red}{\delta t_{u}} - \color{green}{\delta t_{i}})$

::: {.callout-note title="Deriving the pseudorange equation (measurement model)"}
- Based on the expression above, the pseudorange equation (measurement model), using receiver and satellite positions, can be derived
:::

### How to estimate tavel time?

![](assets/figures/correlation.svg)

### How to estimate tavel time? (cont'd)


::: {.columns}

::: {.column}
![](assets/figures/correlation_detail.svg)
:::

::: {.column}
Correlation function ($R$) formula:
$$
R[n] = \sum_{m=0}^{M-1} \color{blue}{c}[n+m] \cdot \color{purple}{r}[m]
$$

- Displacement lag is $n$
- Number of samples is $M$
- The received signal is $\color{purple}{r}[n]$
- The local replica generated at the receiver is $\color{blue}{c}[n]$
:::

:::

### How to estimate tavel time? (cont'd)


::: {.columns}

::: {.column}
::: {style="font-size: 0.75em; line-height: 1.2;"}

Once the correlation peak is found, the travel time can be computed as:
:::

$$
\small
\tau' = n_{peak} \cdot T_{chip}
$$


:::

::: {.column}

::: {style="font-size: 0.75em; line-height: 1.2;"}
Or if a sampling rate $f_s$ greater than $1/T_{chip}$ is used, the travel time can be computed as:
:::
$$
\small
\tau' = \frac{n_{peak}}{f_s}
$$

:::

:::

::: {style="text-align: center;"}

![](assets/figures/correlation_subsampling.svg){height="300"}
:::

### Pseudorange: basic model  {#pseudorange-basic-model}

- Recapitulate, the (simple) pseudorange model for the $i$-th satellite is:

$$
\color{blue}{PR_i} = \underbrace{\sqrt{(\color{red}{x_u} - \color{green}{x_i})^2 + (\color{red}{y_u} - \color{green}{y_i})^2 + (\color{red}{z_u} - \color{green}{z_i})^2}}_{geometric\ range} + \underbrace{c \cdot \color{red}{\delta t_u}}_{clock\ error} + \underbrace{\varepsilon_i}_{noise}
$$

- For the basic model: 4 unknowns: $\color{red}{x_u}, \color{red}{y_u}, \color{red}{z_u}, \color{red}{\delta t_u}$ and 4 equations (from 4 satellites) are needed to solve the system.
- The *noise term* ($\varepsilon_i$) includes all unmodelled errors (e.g. multipath, ionospheric and tropospheric delays, receiver noise, etc.)

### Pseudorange: geometric interpretation


::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="70%"}
![](assets/figures/ranging_errors.svg)
:::

::: {.column width="30%"}
Error terms cause biased measurements (hence the **pseudo** in the range name).
:::

:::

### Carrier-phase: definition


::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="60%"}
![](assets/figures/code_vs_carrier_comparison.svg)
:::

::: {.column width="40%"}

![](assets/figures/phase_shift.svg){height="200"}

$$
\scriptsize
\phi = \mod \left( \frac{\left | \vec{x_u} - \vec{x_i} \right |}{\lambda} , \lambda \right)
$$

::: {style="font-size: 0.75em; line-height: 1.2;"}
Only information within a cycle

[No information (ambiguity) about the number of cycles ($\color{red
}{N}$)!]{style="color:red;"}
:::
:::
:::

### Carrier-phase: basic model

- Similar to the pseudorange model, the carrier-phase observable model:
$$
\color{blue}{\phi_i} = c \cdot \tau'_{i,\phi} = c \cdot \left( \tau_i + \color{red}{\delta t_u} - \color{green}{\delta t_i} \right)
$$

- $\tau'_{i,\phi}$: travel time for the $i$-th satellite as computed by the *phase tracking loop* of the receiver.
- Expanding the expression (as we did for the pseudorange):

$$
\begin{eqnarray}
\color{blue}{\phi_i} &=& \frac{1}{\lambda} \cdot \sqrt{(\color{red}{x_u} - \color{green}{x_i})^2 + (\color{red}{y_u} - \color{green}{y_i})^2 + (\color{red}{z_u} - \color{green}{z_i})^2} +\\
       &+& \color{red}{N_i} + f \cdot \color{red}{\delta t_u} - f \cdot \color{green}{\delta t_i} + \epsilon_{\phi,i}
\end{eqnarray}\quad [cycles]
$$

### Carrier-phase: pseudorange equivalent

- The carrier phase observable can be expressed in pseudorange units by multiplying the carrier-phase observable by the wavelength ($\lambda$):

$$
\begin{eqnarray}
\color{blue}{L_i} &=& \lambda \cdot \color{blue}{\phi_i} =\\
                   & = & \sqrt{(\color{red}{x_u} - \color{green}{x_i})^2 + (\color{red}{y_u} - \color{green}{y_i})^2 + (\color{red}{z_u} - \color{green}{z_i})^2} +\\
       &+& \lambda \cdot \color{red}{N_i} + c \cdot \color{red}{\delta t_u} - c \cdot \color{green}{\delta t_i} + \varepsilon_{\phi,i}
\end{eqnarray}\quad [meters]
$$

- Note that carrier phase adds a new unknown: the integer ambiguity ($\color{red}{N_i}$) for each satellite.
- Carrier phase measurements are much **more precise** (i.e. $\varepsilon_{\phi,i} << \varepsilon_{i}$) than pseudorange, but they are **ambiguous**.

### Doppler: fundamentals

- GNSS receivers can also measure the Doppler shift of the received signal, which leads to the **Doppler observable**

$$
f_{D,i} = -\frac{f_0}{c} \cdot \left (  \underbrace{(\vec{v}_i - \vec{v}_u) \cdot \vec{e_i}}_{\Delta v_{range}} + \frac{\partial}{\partial t}\delta t_u - \frac{\partial}{\partial t}\delta t_i \right ) + \varepsilon_{D,i}
$$

- $\Delta v_{range}$ is the relative velocity between the satellite and the receiver projected onto the line of sight
- $\varepsilon_{D,i}$ is the measurement noise.


### Doppler: geometric interpretation

![](assets/figures/Doppler_interpretation.svg)

- Doppler can be used for velocity estimation and aiding in the positioning process.

### $C/N_0$

- **Carrier-to-Noise density ratio** ($C/N_0$) tells how strong the GNSS signal ($C$ or $P_{carrier}$) is relative to the noise in a 1-Hz bandwidth ($N_0$):

$$
\small
C/N_0 = \frac{P_{carrier}}{N_0} \quad [dB-Hz]
$$

- In \acr{GNSS}, the signal can be trackable even when the \acr{SNR} over the **receiver bandwidth** is  $<0\ dB$, because GNSS receivers exploit correlation/integration with the known *spreading code*.

::: {.callout-warning title="$SNR$ and $C/N_0$ are not the same!"}
However, the term \acr{SNR} is used when in fact $C/N_0$ is being referred to. This is a common source of confusion in the GNSS literature.
:::

## Error sources


![](assets/figures/error_sources.svg)


### Error sources: classification


System errors

- Errors in the navigation message
- Control segment computes the navigation message

Propagation errors

- Uncertainties in the propagation of the signal from the satellite to the receiver

Local errors

- Dependent on the receiver and its environment

### System error sources

- Errors due to the information broadcasted by the satellites in the navigation message:
  - **Ephemeris** errors: errors in the Keplerian parameters that define the satellite orbit
  - Satellite **clock** errors: errors in the satellite clock
    - Satellite clocks are atomic (stable) clocks, but not perfect.
    - The satellite clock is *steered* to the reference time (e.g. GPS time), and the resulting clock offset transmitted in the navigation message.
  - Signal **biases**: errors in the signal generation and transmission process (e.g. group delay, inter-frequency biases, etc.)

### Propagation errors

Propagation delays are due to the interaction of the signal with the atmosphere.

::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

![](assets/figures/atmospheric_layers.svg)


:::

::: {.column}
- Ionosphere + Plasmasphere through the electron density

- Troposphere through the water vapor content
:::
:::


#### Ionosphere error: morphology


::: {.columns}

::: {.column}


Layer of the atmosphere composed of *ionized gases*:

- Located between 70 and 1000 km
- Followed by the plasmasphere (1000-20000 km)
  - Much thinner ionization than the ionosphere
- Ionization due to **solar radiation**. Therefore varies with the Sun:
  - Day and night (i.e. local time) variation
  - Geographic location (i.e. latitude)
  - Solar cycle (Periodicity of 11 year)
:::

::: {.column}
![](assets/figures/iono_layers.svg){height="450"}

- The ionosphere is a *dispersive medium*:
It's effect depends on the signal frequency

:::

:::


#### Ionosphere error: Solar cycle

- Solar activity is measured through the **sunspot number** (SSN), which is a measure of the number of sunspots present on the surface of the Sun.
- At high solar activity, the ionosphere is more ionized, and therefore the propagation delay is higher.

```{python}
import pandas as pd

# Define column widths and names based on the file description
# Year: [1-4], Month: [6-7], Decimal date: [9-16], Smoothed total sunspot number: [19-23],
# Standard deviation: [25-29], Number of observations: [32-35], Definitive/provisional indicator: [37]

colspecs = [
    (0, 4),  # Year
    (5, 7),  # Month
    (8, 16), # Decimal date
    (18, 23), # Smoothed total sunspot number
    (24, 29), # Standard deviation
    (31, 35), # Number of observations
    (36, 37)  # Definitive/provisional indicator
]

column_names = [
    'Year', 'Month', 'Decimal_Date', 'Smoothed_SSN',
    'Standard_Deviation', 'Num_Observations', 'Provisional_Indicator'
]

# Load the data using pandas read_fwf for fixed-width format
# Skip comments at the beginning of the file (lines starting with '#')
df_sunspot = pd.read_fwf(
    'assets/data/SN_ms_tot_V2.0.txt',
    colspecs=colspecs,
    names=column_names,
    comment='#',
    header=None # No header row in the data itself
)

# Create a 'Date' column from 'Year' and 'Month'
df_sunspot['Date'] = pd.to_datetime(df_sunspot['Year'].astype(str) + '-' + df_sunspot['Month'].astype(str) + '-01')

# Convert 'Smoothed_SSN' to numeric, coercing errors
df_sunspot['Smoothed_SSN'] = pd.to_numeric(df_sunspot['Smoothed_SSN'], errors='coerce')

# Drop rows where 'Smoothed_SSN' is NaN (these are likely placeholder values like -1, or parsing errors)
df_sunspot.dropna(subset=['Smoothed_SSN'], inplace=True)
fig = px.line(
    df_sunspot,
    x='Date',
    y='Smoothed_SSN',
    title='Monthly Smoothed Total Sunspot Number Over Time',
    labels={'Date': 'Date', 'Smoothed_SSN': 'Smoothed Sunspot Number'}
)

fig.update_xaxes(rangeslider_visible=True)
HTML(pio.to_html(fig, full_html=False, include_plotlyjs="cdn", include_mathjax=False))
```

#### Ionosphere error: daily variation

- Ionization depends on local time.

![source [UPC/IonSat](https://chapman.upc.es/tomion/real-time/quick/archive.uadg/2026/215/global_vtec_movie_since_last_midnight/)](assets/figures/2026_215_uadg_tec.gif)

- \acr{TEC} Unit: $1\ TECU = 10^{16} \text{electrons/m}^2$

#### Ionosphere error: delay

- Delay ionospheric model for the $i$-th satellite and frequency $f_k$ ($I_i$):

$$
\small
I_i = \frac{40.3}{f_k^2} \cdot \underbrace{\int_{u}^{i} N_e(l) dl}_{TEC_i}
$$

- \acr{TEC} is the integral of the electron density ($N_e$) along the signal path:

- Ionosphere is *dispersive*: frequency dependent
  - Note the $1/f_k^2$ term in the model
  - This is the reason why GNSS use multiple frequencies: to mitigate the ionospheric delay.

- Code delay and phase advance!
  - Same magnitude but opposite sign for code and phase observables

#### Ionosphere error: mapping function


::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

- The slant \acr{TEC} can be derived from the \acr{VTEC} using a mapping function.

$$
\tiny
\begin{eqnarray}
TEC_i &=&  \frac{VTEC_i}{\cos(z')} \\
      &=&  \frac{VTEC_i}{\sqrt{1 - \left(\frac{R_{E}}{R_{E} + h_{m}}\right)^2 \cdot \cos^2(E)}}
\end{eqnarray}
$$

- $E$ is the elevation of the observation
- $h_{m}$ is the effective height of the ionosphere (typically 450 km)
  - Assumption of a thin shell of ionization at a fixed height
:::

::: {.column}
![](assets/figures/mapping_function.svg)
:::

:::


#### Ionosphere error: mapping function

```{python}
import numpy as np

R_earth = 6378.0  # km
h_iono = 450.0    # km, ionospheric effective height

elevation_deg = np.linspace(0.1, 90, 200)
elevation_rad = np.deg2rad(elevation_deg)

z_prime = np.arcsin(R_earth / (R_earth + h_iono) * np.cos(elevation_rad))
mapping_function = 1.0 / np.cos(z_prime)

df_mf = pd.DataFrame({'elevation': elevation_deg, 'mapping_function': mapping_function})

fig = px.line(df_mf, x='elevation', y='mapping_function', title=f'Ionospheric Mapping Function (effective height = {h_iono:.0f} km)', labels={'elevation': 'Elevation angle (deg)', 'mapping_function': 'Mapping function'})
fig.update_layout(xaxis_title='Elevation angle (deg)', yaxis_title='Mapping function')
HTML(pio.to_html(fig, full_html=False, include_plotlyjs="cdn", include_mathjax=False))
```

#### Ionosphere error: models

- GNSS systems provide ionospheric models in the navigation message to correct for the ionospheric delay.
- This is useful for single-frequency receivers
- Different models exist for different GNSS systems:
  - GPS: Klobuchar model (removes around 50% of the ionospheric delay)
  - Galileo: NeQuick model (removes around 70% of the ionospheric delay, [@orus2018status])
  - BeiDou: BDS-2 uses Klobuchar, BDS-3 uses \acr{BDGIM} (removes around 70% of the ionospheric delay, [@yuan2019beidou])
  - GLONASS: no model provided
- Augmentation systems such as \acr{SBAS} also provide ionospheric corrections for single-frequency receivers.
  - They are in general more accurate than the broadcast models, as they are based on a network of reference stations.

#### Ionosphere error: scintillation

- Scintillation is the rapid modification of radio waves caused by small scale structures in the ionosphere.
  - It can prevent a GNSS receiver from locking on to the signal.
  - Strong impact on precise positioning as it can cause cycle slips in the carrier phase observable.

```{python}

df = pd.read_csv('assets/data/LAMP00ITA_S_2024131_snr.csv')


sats = ['E36', 'E09', 'G19', 'G17', 'E05']

df_sats = df[df['sat'].isin(sats)]

# Create a Plotly line chart for SNR over time, with a separate series for each satellite in sats_ok
fig = px.scatter(df_sats, x='epoch', y='snr', color='sat', title='Impact of Scintillation on C/N0 (MATE station, May 10th 2024)')

HTML(pio.to_html(fig, full_html=False, include_plotlyjs="cdn", include_mathjax=False))
```

#### Troposphere error: delay

- Troposphere causes a delay in the GNSS signal due to:
  - dry gases (mainly $N_2$ and $O_2$): *dry component* ($T_{z,dry}$), easy to model
  - water vapour ($H_2O$): *wet component* ($T_{z,wet}$), high variability, complex to model
- Same contribution in code and phase measurements
- Not dispersive: cannot be removed with multiple frequencies
  - Zenith *wet component* usually [estimated]{style="color:red;"} in high precision processing: $\color{red}{d_{wet}}$
  - Usage of *mapping functions* to convert from zenith to slant direction

#### Troposphere error: model

- Tropospheric delay $T_i$ for the $i$-th satellite can be modelled as follows:

$$
T_i = \color{green}{T_{z,dry}} \cdot m_{dry}(E_i) + \color{red}{T_{z,wet}} \cdot m_{wet}(E_i)
$$

$$
\tiny
T_{z,dry} = 0.002277\cdot (1+0.0026 \cdot \cos{2\phi} + 0.00028\cdot H) \cdot P_0
$$

$$
\tiny
m_{dry}(E) = \frac{1}{\sin{E} + \frac{0.00143}{\tan{E}+0.0445}};\ m_{wet}(E) = \frac{1}{\sin{E} + \frac{0.00035}{\tan{E}+0.017}}
$$

::: {.callout-note title="One tropo unknwon per user!"}
As a local effect and thanks to the mapping function, only one additional unknown per receiver
:::

### Local error sources

Local error sources are due to the receiver and its environment:

- Clock errors: receiver clock is not perfectly synchronized with the GNSS system time
- Multipath: signal is reflected by nearby objects before reaching the receiver
- Receiver noise: thermal noise in the receiver electronics

#### Clock error: synchronization jumps

- Local clock errors are due to the receiver's clock not being perfectly synchronized with the GNSS system time.
- Some old receivers (manufacurer dependent) showed clock jumps

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
from pygnss import rinex
import plotly.graph_objects as go
import pandas as pd

rnx_file_path = 'assets/data/UNSA00XXX_R_20142150000_01D_05M_MO.rnx'
obs = rinex.to_dataframe(rnx_file_path)

obs_clean = obs.dropna(subset=['epoch', 'range'])
obs_clean = obs_clean[obs_clean['channel']== '1C']

fig = px.scatter(obs_clean, x='epoch', y='range', color='sat', height=300)


fig.update_layout(
    title=f'Pseudorange Data (Clock millisecond jumps) - UNSA station',
    xaxis_title='Time',
    yaxis_title='Pseudorange (meters)',
    hovermode='x unified'
)

HTML(pio.to_html(fig, full_html=False, include_plotlyjs="cdn", include_mathjax=False))
```

::: {.fragment}
- Good news: common across-satellite effects are absorved by the clock
:::

#### Clock error: model and magnitude

- The receiver clock error is a **bias** in the pseudorange and carrier phase measurements
- It is usually **estimated** as an additional unknown in the positioning process
- Estimation accuracy
  - For a target positioning error of $\pm 1$ m, the receiver clock error must be estimated with an accuracy of $\pm 3.3$ ns

$$
\tau = \frac{p_{error}}{c} = \frac{1\ m}{3 \cdot 10^8\ m/s} \simeq 3.3\ ns
$$

#### Multipath

Reception of the signal through different paths so that we
receive the direct signal plus several delayed and attenuated versions.

- The main effect is a **distortion of the correlation curve** and phase of the
received signal
- Different error for each satellite (amplitude, delay and phase)
  - Difficult to model
- Mitigation techniques:
  - Narrow-Correlator spacing
  - Multipath Estimating DLL (MEDLL)
  - Antenna arrays
  - New GNSS signals with multipath mitigation techniques (e.g. Galileo E1C, E5a, E5b, E6B)


#### Multipath (cont'd)

![](assets/figures/multipath.svg)


#### Receiver noise

As in every RF receiver \acr{AWGN} is present:

- Antenna noise
- Receiver noise temperature
- Quantization noise

Observable noises, when sufficient \acr{SNR}:

- Code measurements are noisy (≈ 1 m)
- Phase measurements are precise (≈ 1% cycle≈ 2 mm)

#### Receiver noise (cont'd)

- Observable noise depend inversely on the \acr{C/N0} of the received signal (see Section 14.6 of [@teunissen2017springer]):

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="60%"}
$$
\small
\sigma_{code} \simeq c \cdot T_{chip} \sqrt {\frac{BW_{DLL} \cdot d_{E-L}}{2\cdot C/N_0}} \quad [m]
$$

$$
\small
\sigma_{phase}  \simeq \frac{\lambda}{2\pi} \sqrt {\frac{BW_{PLL}}{C/N_0}} \quad [m]
$$
:::

::: {.column width="40%"}
- where:
  - $T_{chip}$: chip period of the spreading code (e.g. 1/1.023 MHz for GPS C/A code)
  - $d_{E-L}$: early-late correlator spacing (in chips)
  - $BW_{DLL}$: bandwidth of the code tracking loop (in Hz)
  - $BW_{PLL}$: bandwidth of the carrier tracking loop (in Hz)
  - $C/N_0$: carrier-to-noise density ratio (in Hz)
:::

:::

#### Receiver noise: code tracking

```{python}
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

c = 3e8              # speed of light [m/s]
T_chip = 1 / 1.023e6  # GPS C/A code chip period [s]
d_EL = 1.0            # early-late correlator spacing [chips]

cn0_db = np.linspace(20, 50, 200)
cn0_lin = 10 ** (cn0_db / 10)

bw_dll_values = [0.5, 1.0, 2.0]  # Hz, typical DLL bandwidths

rows = []
for bw_dll in bw_dll_values:
    sigma_code = c * T_chip * np.sqrt(bw_dll * d_EL / (2 * cn0_lin))
    rows.append(pd.DataFrame({'CN0': cn0_db, 'sigma_code': sigma_code, 'BW_DLL': f'{bw_dll} Hz'}))

df_code = pd.concat(rows, ignore_index=True)

fig = px.line(df_code, x='CN0', y='sigma_code', color='BW_DLL',
              title=f'Code tracking noise vs C/N0 (early-late spacing = {d_EL:.1f} chip)',
              labels={'CN0': 'C/N0 (dB-Hz)', 'sigma_code': 'Code noise std. dev. (m)', 'BW_DLL': 'DLL bandwidth'})
fig.update_layout(xaxis_title='C/N0 (dB-Hz)', yaxis_title='Code noise σ (m)')
HTML(pio.to_html(fig, full_html=False, include_plotlyjs="cdn", include_mathjax=False))
```

#### Receiver noise: phase tracking

```{python}
lambda_L1 = c / 1575.42e6  # GPS L1 wavelength [m]

bw_pll_values = [5.0, 10.0, 15.0]  # Hz, typical PLL bandwidths

rows = []
for bw_pll in bw_pll_values:
    sigma_phase = lambda_L1 / (2 * np.pi) * np.sqrt(bw_pll / cn0_lin)
    rows.append(pd.DataFrame({'CN0': cn0_db, 'sigma_phase': sigma_phase * 1000, 'BW_PLL': f'{bw_pll} Hz'}))

df_phase = pd.concat(rows, ignore_index=True)

fig = px.line(df_phase, x='CN0', y='sigma_phase', color='BW_PLL',
              title='Carrier-phase tracking noise vs C/N0',
              labels={'CN0': 'C/N0 (dB-Hz)', 'sigma_phase': 'Phase noise std. dev. (mm)', 'BW_PLL': 'PLL bandwidth'})
fig.update_layout(xaxis_title='C/N0 (dB-Hz)', yaxis_title='Phase noise σ (mm)')
HTML(pio.to_html(fig, full_html=False, include_plotlyjs="cdn", include_mathjax=False))
```

### Measurement model

- Recall the [basic pseudorange model](#pseudorange-basic-model)
- Once we have defined all the error sources, we can now rewrite the range models,
specially the terms hidden under
  - **noise** ($\varepsilon_i$) in the pseudorange model
  - **noise** ($\varepsilon_{\phi,i}$) in the carrier-phase model
- In the following models, the following convention has been adopted:
  - $k$ is the frequency index (e.g. $k=1$ for L1, $k=2$ for L2, etc.)
  - $i$ is the satellite index
  - $s$ is the signal index (e.g. $s=1$ for C/A, $s=2$ for P(Y), etc.)
  - Color coding consistent with the previous section plus:
    - $\color{cyan}{value}$: indicate a term that can be modeled or estimated.

### Measurement model: pseudorange

$$
\begin{eqnarray}
\color{blue}{PR_i} & =& \underbrace{\sqrt{(\color{red}{x_u} - \color{green}{x_i})^2 + (\color{red}{y_u} - \color{green}{y_i})^2 + (\color{red}{z_u} - \color{green}{z_i})^2}}_{geometric\ range} + \\
  & & \underbrace{c \cdot \color{red}{\delta t_u}}_{rx\ clock\ error} - \underbrace{c \cdot \color{green}{\delta t_i}}_{sat\ clock\ error}+ \\
  & & \underbrace{\frac{40.3}{f_{k,i}^2}\cdot \color{cyan}{TEC_i}}_{ionosphere} + \underbrace{\color{cyan}{T_i}}_{troposphere} + \\
  & & \underbrace{K_{u,s} -K_{i,s}}_{code\ instrumental\ delays} + \underbrace{M_{k,s}}_{multipath} + \underbrace{\varepsilon_i}_{noise}
\end{eqnarray}
$$

### Measurement model: carrier-phase


$$
\begin{eqnarray}
\color{blue}{L_i} & =& \underbrace{\sqrt{(\color{red}{x_u} - \color{green}{x_i})^2 + (\color{red}{y_u} - \color{green}{y_i})^2 + (\color{red}{z_u} - \color{green}{z_i})^2}}_{geometric\ range} + \\
  & & \underbrace{c \cdot \color{red}{\delta t_u}}_{rx\ clock\ error} - \underbrace{c \cdot \color{green}{\delta t_i}}_{sat\ clock\ error} - \\
  & & \underbrace{\frac{40.3}{f_{k,i}^2}\cdot \color{cyan}{TEC_i}}_{ionosphere} + \underbrace{\color{cyan}{T_i}}_{troposphere} + \\
  & & \underbrace{k_{u,s} -k_{i,s}}_{phase\ instrumental\ delays} + \underbrace{m_{k,s}}_{multipath} + \underbrace{\lambda \cdot \color{green}{w_{k,i}}}_{wind-up} + \underbrace{\color{red}{N_{k,i}}}_{ambiguity} + \underbrace{\varepsilon_i}_{noise}
\end{eqnarray}
$$


## Observable combinations

Observable combination allow to **cancel** errors or **isolate** specific terms of the range and phase models

- To simplify notation, the combination will use

$$
\small
\rho_i=\sqrt{(x_u - x_i)^2 + (y_u - y_i)^2 + (z_u - z_i)^2}
$$

- therefore the range model becomes:

$$
\small
PR_i = \rho_i + c \cdot \delta t_u - c \cdot \delta t_i + \frac{40.3}{f_{k,i}^2} \cdot TEC_i + T_i + K_{u,s} - K_{i,s} + M_{k,s} + \varepsilon_i
$$


### Iono-free combination: definition

- Iono free combination is used to **remove the ionospheric delay**. For two observables ($PR_a$, $PR_b$) taken at frequencies $f_a$ and $f_b$:

$$
\small
\begin{eqnarray}
PR_{i, PC} &=& \frac{f_a^2 \cdot PR_{i,a} - f_b^2 \cdot PR_{i,b}}{f_a^2 - f_b^2} \\
       & = & \rho_i + c \cdot \delta t_u - c \cdot \delta t_i + T_i + K_{PC, u} - K_{PC, i} + M_{PC, i} + \varepsilon_{PC,i} \\
       & & \\
L_{i, PC} &=& \frac{f_a^2 \cdot L_{i,a} - f_b^2 \cdot L_{i,b}}{f_a^2 - f_b^2} \\
       & = & \rho_i + c \cdot \delta t_u - c \cdot \delta t_i + T_i + k_{PC, u} - k_{PC, i} + m_{PC, i} + c \cdot w_{PC,i} + \\
       &  & + N_{PC} + \varepsilon_{\phi, PC,i} \\
\end{eqnarray}
$$

### Iono-free combination: combined terms

- Note that frequency/signal dependent terms will be a combination of the raw measurements:


$$
\tiny
\begin{array}{cc}
\textbf{Code} & \textbf{Phase} \\[1ex]
\begin{aligned}
K_{PC,u} &=
\frac{f_a^2 K_{u,a}-f_b^2 K_{u,b}}
     {f_a^2-f_b^2}
\\[1ex]
K_{PC,i} &=
\frac{f_a^2 K_{i,a}-f_b^2 K_{i,b}}
     {f_a^2-f_b^2}
\\[1ex]
M_{PC,i} &=
\frac{f_a^2 M_{i,a}-f_b^2 M_{i,b}}
     {f_a^2-f_b^2}
\\[1ex]
\varepsilon_{PC,i} &=
\frac{f_a^2\varepsilon_{i,a}-f_b^2\varepsilon_{i,b}}
     {f_a^2-f_b^2}
\end{aligned}
&
\begin{aligned}
k_{PC,u} &=
\frac{f_a^2 k_{u,a}-f_b^2 k_{u,b}}
     {f_a^2-f_b^2}
\\[1ex]
k_{PC,i} &=
\frac{f_a^2 k_{i,a}-f_b^2 k_{i,b}}
     {f_a^2-f_b^2}
\\[1ex]
m_{PC,i} &=
\frac{f_a^2 m_{i,a}-f_b^2 m_{i,b}}
     {f_a^2-f_b^2}
\\[1ex]
N_{PC} &=
\frac{f_a^2\lambda_a N_a-f_b^2\lambda_b N_b}
     {f_a^2-f_b^2}
\end{aligned}
\end{array}
$$

### Iono-free combination: takeaways

- The $N_a$ and $N_b$ in the *raw* observables are integer, but the combined one $N_{PC}$ is not
  - This is critical for high accuracy positioning
  - When computing position using this combination, this term is *floated* first (estimated as a float), and then attempt *ambiguity resolution*

- Ionosphere is gone, but **noise increases**!
  - If we assume equal noise on the two frequencies ($\sigma_1 = \sigma_2 = \sigma$), and GPS frequencies ($f_a = f_1 = 1575.42\,MHz$ and $f_b = f_2 = 1227.60\,MHz$), the amplification factor is


$$
\small
\begin{eqnarray}
\sigma_{PC} &= &
\sqrt{
\left(
\frac{f_a^2}{f_a^2-f_b^2}
\right)^2 \sigma_1^2
+
\left(
\frac{f_b^2}{f_a^2-f_b^2}
\right)^2 \sigma_2^2
} & & \\
\left. \sigma_{PC} \right|_{\sigma_1=\sigma_2=\sigma,f_1,f_2} &=&
\sqrt{2.546^2+1.546^2}\,\sigma
& \approx &
2.98\,\sigma
\end{eqnarray}
$$


### Geometry-free combination: definition

- Removes non-frequency dependent terms
- Assuming frequencies $f_a$ and $f_b$, where $f_a > f_b$


$$
\small
\begin{eqnarray}
PR_{i,GF} &=& PR_{i,b}-PR_{i,a} ⚠️ \\
&=&
40.3
\left(
\frac{1}{f_b^2}-\frac{1}{f_a^2}
\right) TEC_i
+
K_{GF,u}-K_{GF,i}
+
M_{GF,i}
+
\varepsilon_{GF,i}
\end{eqnarray}
$$

$$
\small
\begin{eqnarray}
L_{i,GF} &=& L_{i,a}-L_{i,b} \\
&=&
40.3
\left(
\frac{1}{f_b^2}-\frac{1}{f_a^2}
\right) TEC_i
+
k_{GF,u}-k_{GF,i}
+
m_{GF,i}
+
c\cdot w_{GF,i} \\
&&
+
N_{GF}
+
\varepsilon_{\phi,GF,i}
\end{eqnarray}
$$

### Geometry-free combination: combined terms


$$
\small
\begin{array}{cc}
\textbf{Code} & \textbf{Phase} \\[1ex]
\begin{aligned}
K_{GF,u} &= K_{u,b}-K_{u,a}
\\
K_{GF,i} &= K_{i,b}-K_{i,a}
\\
M_{GF,i} &= M_{i,b}-M_{i,a}
\\
\varepsilon_{GF,i} &=
\varepsilon_{i,a}-\varepsilon_{i,b}
\end{aligned}
&
\begin{aligned}
k_{GF,u} &= k_{u,a}-k_{u,b}
\\
k_{GF,i} &= k_{i,a}-k_{i,b}
\\
m_{GF,i} &= m_{i,a}-m_{i,b}
\\
N_{GF} &= N_a-N_b
\end{aligned}
\end{array}
$$

- Main takeaways
  - Noise amplified by a factor of $\sqrt{2}$
  - Ambiguity $N_{GF}$ keeps its integer nature

### Geometry-free: data interpretation


```{python}
import numpy as np

c = 299792458.0  # speed of light [m/s]
lambda_a = c / 1575.42e6  # GPS L1 wavelength [m]
lambda_b = c / 1227.60e6  # GPS L2 wavelength [m]

df = rinex.to_dataframe('assets/data/EBRE00ESP_R_20260590000_01D_30S_GO.rnx')

channel_a = "1C"
channel_b = "2W"

df_case = df[(df['sat'] == sat) & ((df['channel'] == channel_a) | (df['channel'] == channel_b))]

df_gf = df_case.pivot(
    index=["epoch", "constellation", "sat", "station"],

df_gf.columns = [
    f"{observable}_{channel}"
    for observable, channel in df_gf.columns
]

df_gf = df_gf.reset_index()

# Geometry-free combination: code and phase residuals for a single satellite
range_gf = df_gf['range_2W'] - df_gf['range_1C']
phase_gf = df_gf['phase_1C'] * lambda_a - df_gf['phase_2W'] * lambda_b + 12

fig = go.Figure()

fig.add_trace(

fig.update_layout(
    template='plotly_white',
```

### Narrow- and wide-lane combinations

::: {style="text-size: 0.8em;"}
- These combinations linearly combine the carrier-phase observables to create a new effective wavelength.
  - Used in the ambiguity resolution process, as they are more sensitive to cycle slips than the original observables.
  - Neither combination removes the ionospheric delay. Their effective wavelengths are $\lambda_{WL}=c/(f_a-f_b)$ and $\lambda_{NL}=c/(f_a+f_b)$.
:::

::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

[Wide lane $L_{WL}$]{style="text-size: 0.8em;"}

$$
\tiny
\begin{eqnarray}
PR_{WL} &=& \frac{f_a \cdot PR_a - f_b \cdot PR_b}{f_a - f_b} \\
L_{WL} &=& \frac{f_a \cdot L_a - f_b \cdot L_b}{f_a - f_b}
\end{eqnarray}
$$
:::

::: {.column}

[Narrow lane $L_{NL}$]{style="text-size: 0.8em;"}

$$
\tiny
\begin{eqnarray}
PR_{NL} &=& \frac{f_a \cdot PR_a + f_b \cdot PR_b}{f_a + f_b} \\
L_{NL} &=& \frac{f_a \cdot L_a + f_b \cdot L_b}{f_a + f_b}
\end{eqnarray}
$$
:::

:::



### Other combinations

- [Additional combinations](https://gssc.esa.int/navipedia/index.php/Combination_of_GNSS_Measurements) used to mitigate/analyze specific error sources:

  - Single frequency  \acr{GRAPHIC}
    - Removes geometry exposing the ionospheric delay (for single-frequency receivers)
  - Multipath combination ($PR_{MP}$, see [@montenbruck2003flight])
    - isolates multipath error in the code measurement

$$
\tiny
PR_{MP} = PR_a
-\frac{2}{f_a^2-f_b^2}
\left(
f_a^2 L_b-f_b^2 L_a
\right)
-L_a
-B_a
$$

### Observable smoothing: definition

- Can we obtain a measurement that is both **precise** (*carrier-phase*)and **unambiguous** (*code pseudorange*)? Hatch filter

$$
\begin{eqnarray}
\tilde{R}[n;k]  & = & \frac{1}{m}\cdot R[n;k] + \\
                &  & \frac{m-1}{m}\left[\tilde{R}[m:k-1] + (\Phi[n:k] - \Phi[n:k-1])\right]
\end{eqnarray}
$$

::: {.callout-warning title="Hatch filter must be initialized on every **cycle slip**!"}
:::

### Observable smoothing: example

```{python}
df = rinex.to_dataframe('assets/data/EBRE00ESP_R_20260592000_04H_30S_GO.rnx')

def hatch_filter(P, phi, N=10):
    """Hatch carrier-smoothed pseudorange."""

    result = np.empty(len(P))
    result[0] = P[0]

    for k in range(1, len(P)):
        result[k] = (
            P[k] / N
            + (N - 1) / N
            * (result[k - 1] + phi[k] - phi[k - 1])
        )

    return result

sat = 'G06'
channel_a = '1C'
channel_b = '2W'

df_case = df[(df['sat'] == sat) & ((df['channel'] == channel_a) | (df['channel'] == channel_b))]

df_gf = df_case.pivot(
    index=["epoch", "constellation", "sat", "station"],
    columns="channel",
    values=["range", "phase", "doppler", "snr", "slip"]
)
df_gf.columns = [
    f"{observable}_{channel}"
    for observable, channel in df_gf.columns
]
df_gf = df_gf.reset_index()

code_gf = df_gf['range_2W'] - df_gf['range_1C']
phi_gf = df_gf['phase_1C'] * lambda_a - df_gf['phase_2W'] * lambda_b

hatch_short = hatch_filter(code_gf.to_numpy(), phi_gf.to_numpy(), N=3)
hatch_long = hatch_filter(code_gf.to_numpy(), phi_gf.to_numpy(), N=30)

fig = go.Figure()

fig.add_trace(
    go.Scatter(
        x=df_gf['epoch'],
        y=code_gf,
        mode='markers',
        name='Unsmoothed code',
        marker={'size': 5, 'color': '#7f8c8d', 'opacity': 0.8},
        hovertemplate='Epoch: %{x}<br>Code GF: %{y:.2f} m<extra></extra>'
    )
)

fig.add_trace(
    go.Scatter(
        x=df_gf['epoch'],
        y=phi_gf,
        mode='markers',
        name='Carrier phase',
        marker={'size': 5, 'color': '#e67e22', 'opacity': 0.8},
        hovertemplate='Epoch: %{x}<br>Phase GF: %{y:.2f} m<extra></extra>'
    )
)

fig.add_trace(
    go.Scatter(
        x=df_gf['epoch'],
        y=hatch_short,
        mode='lines+markers',
        name='Smoothed (N=3)',
        line={'color': '#2e86de', 'width': 2},
        marker={'size': 4, 'color': '#2e86de', 'opacity': 0.8},
        hovertemplate='Epoch: %{x}<br>Smoothed (m=3): %{y:.2f} m<extra></extra>'
    )
)

fig.add_trace(
    go.Scatter(
        x=df_gf['epoch'],
        y=hatch_long,
        mode='lines+markers',
        name='Smoothed (N=30)',
        line={'color': '#27ae60', 'width': 2},
        marker={'size': 4, 'color': '#27ae60', 'opacity': 0.8},
        hovertemplate='Epoch: %{x}<br>Smoothed (m=30): %{y:.2f} m<extra></extra>'
    )
)

fig.update_layout(
    template='plotly_white',
    title='Carrier-smoothed pseudorange using the Hatch filter',
    xaxis_title='Epoch [s]',
    yaxis_title='Geometry-free observable [m]',
    legend_title_text='Observable',
    hovermode='x unified',
    margin=dict(l=60, r=20, t=60, b=50),
    height=450,
    width=900,
)

fig.update_xaxes(showgrid=True, gridcolor='lightgray')
fig.update_yaxes(showgrid=True, gridcolor='lightgray')

HTML(pio.to_html(fig, full_html=False, include_plotlyjs='cdn', include_mathjax=False))
```

## Cycle slips

- Cycle slips are **sudden changes in the integer ambiguity** of the carrier phase observable
- They can be caused by:
  - Loss of lock due to low signal strength or interference
  - Receiver resets or clock jumps
  - Multipath effects
  - Ionospheric scintillation
- Whenever a cycle slip occurs, the ambiguity term $N_{k,i}$ needs to be re-estimated, which can lead to positioning errors if not properly handled.
- Examples of cycle slips can be found in the [geometry-free combination](#geometry-free-data-interpretation) of the carrier phase observable.

## Navigation solution

This section covers the inner workings of a **positioning engine**:

::: {style="text-align: center;"}
*How to translate from measurements to positions?*
:::

- In simplistic terms, let $\mathbf{z} = (z_1, ..., z_N)^\mathsf{T}$ be the measurement vector and let $\mathbf{x}$ be the estimation state. The state contains every unknown being estimated, not only the receiver position:

$$
\mathbf{z} = h(\mathbf{x}) \Longrightarrow \hat{\mathbf{x}} = \underset{\mathbf{x}}{\operatorname{arg\,min}}\;\|\mathbf{z}-h(\mathbf{x})\|
$$

- The receiver position will be in general only one part of the state:

### Navigation solution: linearization

- Problem: *norm* operator is **nonlinear**:

$$
\rho_i = \sqrt{(x_i-x_u)^2+(y_i-y_u)^2+(z_i-z_u)^2}
$$

- Solution: use a **first-order Taylor approximation** around an
  *a-priori* state $\mathbf{x}_0$ (e.g. an approximate state)

$$
\small
\begin{eqnarray}
h(\mathbf{x}_u) & \approx & h(\mathbf{x}_0) + \mathbf{H}(\mathbf{x}_0) (\mathbf{x}_u-\mathbf{x}_0) \\
          & = & h(\mathbf{x}_0) + \mathbf{H}(\mathbf{x}_0) \cdot \Delta \mathbf{x}_u
\end{eqnarray}
$$

### Navigation solution: linearization (cont'd)

- For the range to a known $i$-th satellite position $\vec s_i$,

$$
\tiny
f(x,y,z) = f(x_0, y_0, z_0) + \frac{\partial f(x_0, y_0, z_0)}{\partial x} \cdot \Delta x + \frac{\partial f(x_0, y_0, z_0)}{\partial y} \cdot \Delta y + \frac{\partial f(x_0, y_0, z_0)}{\partial z} \cdot \Delta z
$$

- Convention: from receiver to satellite $\vec s_i - \vec p_u$ and not $\vec p_u - \vec s_i$

$$
\small
\begin{eqnarray}
\frac{\partial f(x_0, y_0, z_0)}{\partial x} & = &  \frac{\partial}{\partial x} \sqrt{(x_i-x_0)^2+(y_i-y_0)^2+(z_i-z_0)^2} \\
                & =&  \frac{(x_i - x_0)}{\sqrt{(x_i-x_0)^2+(y_i-y_0)^2+(z_i-z_0)^2}} = \frac{(x_i - x_0)}{\rho_{i,0}}
\end{eqnarray}
$$

### Navigation solution: linearization (cont'd)

- Putting it all together:

$$
\small
\rho_i = \rho_{i,0} - \frac{(x_i - x_0)}{\rho_{i,0}} \Delta x - \frac{(y_i - y_0)}{\rho_{i,0}} \Delta y - \frac{(z_i - z_0)}{\rho_{i,0}} \Delta z
$$

::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-warning title="Why sign reversal?"}
- Gradient function is defined as **maximum increase** of the function
- Convention taken: from receiver to satellite
  - If receiver moves towards the satellite, range decreases (i.e. opposite of gradient convention)
:::
:::

### Navigation solution: linear equations

- Once linearization is achieved, we can fetch the [pseudorange basic model](#pseudorange-basic-model) (for now) and convert it to their linear version for 4 satellites:


$$
\small
\begin{eqnarray}
\color{blue}{PR_1} = \rho_{1,0} - \frac{(x_1 - x_0)}{\rho_{1,0}} \color{red}{\Delta x} - \frac{(y_1 - y_0)}{\rho_{1,0}} \color{red}{\Delta y} - \frac{(z_1 - z_0)}{\rho_{1,0}} \color{red}{\Delta z} + c \cdot \color{red}{\delta t_u} \\
\color{blue}{PR_2} = \rho_{1,0} - \frac{(x_2 - x_0)}{\rho_{1,0}} \color{red}{\Delta x} - \frac{(y_2 - y_0)}{\rho_{1,0}} \color{red}{\Delta y} - \frac{(z_2 - z_0)}{\rho_{1,0}} \color{red}{\Delta z} + c \cdot \color{red}{\delta t_u} \\
\color{blue}{PR_3} = \rho_{1,0} - \frac{(x_3 - x_0)}{\rho_{1,0}} \color{red}{\Delta x} - \frac{(y_3 - y_0)}{\rho_{1,0}} \color{red}{\Delta y} - \frac{(z_3 - z_0)}{\rho_{1,0}} \color{red}{\Delta z} + c \cdot \color{red}{\delta t_u} \\
\color{blue}{PR_4} = \rho_{1,0} - \frac{(x_4 - x_0)}{\rho_{1,0}} \color{red}{\Delta x} - \frac{(y_4 - y_0)}{\rho_{1,0}} \color{red}{\Delta y} - \frac{(z_4 - z_0)}{\rho_{1,0}} \color{red}{\Delta z} + c \cdot \color{red}{\delta t_u} \\
\end{eqnarray}
$$


### Navigation solution: linear system

- Rearranging:  $\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{H}_k\cdot \Delta\mathbf{x}$, where $\mathbf{H}_k$ is the linearized measurement model at epoch $k$.

$$
\tiny
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} PR_1 - \rho_{1,0} \\ PR_2 - \rho_{2,0} \\ PR_3 - \rho_{3,0} \\ PR_4 - \rho_{4,0} \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf{y}\;\mathrm{(prefit\ residuals)}} = \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} -\frac{(x_1 - x_0)}{\rho_{1,0}} & -\frac{(y_1 - y_0)}{\rho_{1,0}} & -\frac{(z_1 - z_0)}{\rho_{1,0}} & 1 \\ -\frac{(x_2 - x_0)}{\rho_{2,0}} & -\frac{(y_2 - y_0)}{\rho_{2,0}} & -\frac{(z_2 - z_0)}{\rho_{2,0}} & 1 \\ -\frac{(x_3 - x_0)}{\rho_{3,0}} & -\frac{(y_3 - y_0)}{\rho_{3,0}} & -\frac{(z_3 - z_0)}{\rho_{3,0}} & 1 \\ -\frac{(x_4 - x_0)}{\rho_{4,0}} & -\frac{(y_4 - y_0)}{\rho_{4,0}} & -\frac{(z_4 - z_0)}{\rho_{4,0}} & 1 \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf{H}_k\;\mathrm{(measurement\ Jacobian)}} \cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} \color{red}{\Delta x} \\ \color{red}{\Delta y} \\ \color{red}{\Delta z} \\ \color{red}{\Delta b_u} \end{bmatrix}}_{\Delta\mathbf{x}}
$$

- ⚠️ The solver estimates a correction relative to the a-priori state:
  - $\Delta\mathbf{x} = [\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z, c \cdot \delta t_u]^\mathsf{T} \Rightarrow \mathbf{x}_u = \mathbf{x}_0 + \Delta\mathbf{x}$
- This is the simplest solution of the navigation problem: \acr{SPP}

### Navigation solution: overdetermined systems

- What to do when number of satellites $>4 \longrightarrow \mathbf{H}_k$ is not square, therefore not invertible!
- Use of the [*Moore-Penrose inverse*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moore%E2%80%93Penrose_inverse) (aka *pseudoinverse*)

$$
\Delta\mathbf{x} = \left ( \mathbf{H}_k^T\cdot \mathbf{H}_k \right)^{-1} \mathbf{H}_k^T \cdot \mathbf{y}
$$

### Navigation solution: weighting observations

- What if some measurements are more *trustworthy* than others?
  - Mathematically, more *trustworthy* means lower $\sigma_{\varepsilon}$.

- With the $N$ noise variances we can build the *weighting matrix*:

$$
\mathbf{W} = diag\left ( \sigma_{\varepsilon,1}^{-2} \dots \sigma_{\varepsilon,i}^{-2} \dots \sigma_{\varepsilon,N}^{-2} \right )
$$

- And the full pseudoinverse with weighting matrix can be computed as:

$$
\Delta\mathbf{x} = \left ( \mathbf{H}_k^T\cdot \mathbf{W} \cdot \mathbf{H}_k \right)^{-1} \mathbf{H}_k^T \cdot \mathbf{W} \cdot \mathbf{y}
$$


## Positioning error

- Solution provided by the positioning engine is not perfect, it is driven by
  - **quality of the measurements** (or measurement error, i.e. $\varepsilon$)
  - **geometry of the satellites**

- The resulting error of the positioning engine can be quantified by the **covariance matrix** of the solution:
  - the diagonal elements are the variances of the estimated state
  - the off-diagonal elements are the covariances between the estimated states, and can be used to assess the correlation between the estimated states


### User Equivalent Range Error

- The \acr{UERE} is a measure of the total error in the range measurements (i.e. *along-range* errors)
- The $\sigma_{UERE,i}^2$ for the $i$-th satellite can be computed as the sum square of the individual error sources:

$$
\small
\sigma_{UERE,i}^2 =
\underbrace{\sigma_{I,i}^2}_{ionosphere} +
\underbrace{\sigma_{T,i}^2}_{troposphere} +
\underbrace{\sigma_{s,i}^2}_{satellite\ clock} +
\underbrace{\sigma_{e,i}^2}_{satellite\ ephemeris} +
\underbrace{\sigma_{r,i}^2}_{receiver\ errors}
$$

- Note that the different  $\sigma_{UERE}^2$ are in fact the $\sigma_{\varepsilon}^2$ used in the weighting matrix of the pseudoinverse solution.

### UERE: error budget

- The different error components of the \acr{UERE} are summarized in the following table:


| Error source | Min typ. value (m) | Max typ. value (m) |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Ionosphere | 2 | 10 |
| Troposphere | 0.2 | 1.0 |
| Satellite clock | 0.5 | 1.0 |
| Satellite ephemeris | 0.5 | 1.0 |
| Receiver errors (multipath) | 0.5 | 2.0 |
| Receiver errors (thermal noise) | 0.1 | 1.0 |
| **UERE** | **2.2** | **10.4** |


### Dilution of Precision

- The \acr{GDOP} is a measure of the *geometry* of the satellites
- It has a multiplicative effect on the positioning error

![](assets/figures/gdop.svg)


### Dilution of Precision: computation

- The \acr{GDOP} can be computed from the measurement Jacobian $\mathbf{H}_k$ of the linearized system.
  - It depends only on the geometry of the satellites at the observation epoch, and not on the measurements themselves
- The \acr{DOP} geometry matrix ${\bf G}$ is computed as:

$$
\mathbf{G} =\left ( \mathbf{H}_k^T\cdot \mathbf{H}_k \right )^{-1} =
\begin{bmatrix}
\color{crimson}{\sigma_x}^2 & \sigma_{xy}^2 & \sigma_{xz}^2 & \sigma_{xt}^2 \\
\sigma_{xy}^2 & \color{crimson}{\sigma_y}^2 & \sigma_{yz}^2 & \sigma_{yt}^2 \\
\sigma_{xz}^2 & \sigma_{yz}^2 & \color{crimson}{\sigma_z}^2 & \sigma_{zt}^2 \\
\sigma_{xt}^2 & \sigma_{yt}^2 & \sigma_{zt}^2 & \color{crimson}{\sigma_t}^2
\end{bmatrix}
$$

### Dilution of Precision: flavors

- The \acr{GDOP} is a generalization of the \acr{DOP} concept, which can be computed for different subsets of the estimated state:

$$
\begin{eqnarray}
PDOP &=& \sqrt{\sigma_x^2 + \sigma_y^2 + \sigma_z^2 + \sigma_t^2} \\
HDOP &=& \sqrt{\sigma_x^2 + \sigma_y^2} \\
VDOP &=& \sqrt{\sigma_z^2} \\
TDOP &=& \sqrt{\sigma_t^2}
\end{eqnarray}
$$

### Dilution of Precision: values

- The \acr{GDOP} is a unitless quantity, and its value can be interpreted as follows (source [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dilution_of_precision))

| DOP value | Rating | Description |
|:---------:|:------:|:----------- |
| < 1 | Ideal | Highest possible confidence level and precision |
| 1–2 | Excellent | Positions are accurate enough to meet all but the most sensitive applications |
| 2–5 | Good | Minimum appropriate for making accurate decisions. Positions could be used to make reliable in-route navigation suggestions to the user |
| 5–10 | Moderate | A more open view of the sky is recommended. Positions could be used for calculations, but the fix quality could still be improved |
| 10–20 | Fair | Positions should be discarded or used only to indicate a very rough estimate of the current location |
| > 20 | Poor | Solutions should be discarded. |

### Positioning error from GDOP and UERE

- The approximate covariance matrix of the positioning solution ($\Sigma_{pos}$) can be computed as:

$$
\Sigma_{pos} = \sigma_{UERE}^2 \cdot {\bf G}
$$

- And a rough estimate of the positioning error can be obtained by multiplying the \acr{UERE} with the \acr{GDOP}:

$$
\sigma_{pos} \approx \sigma_{UERE} \cdot GDOP
$$

## Precise positioning

This section covers the different techniques used to achieve **high accuracy positioning** (beyond \acr{SPP}).

It includes the following main content:

- **Kalman filter** as the foundation of high accuracy positioning engines
- Various techniques to improve the positioning solution:
  - **PPP**: using precise satellite orbit and clock information to achieve decimeter-level accuracy
  - **RTK**: using carrier phase measurements to achieve centimeter-level accuracy

### Kalman Filter: key idea

::: {style="text-align: center;"}
*How can we combine noisy measurements with what we already know about the motion?*
:::

<hr style="border: 1px solid #cccccc; margin: 20px 0;">

The **Kalman filter** combines, at every time step, two sources of **imperfect** information.

  - **Prediction**: Use the knowledge of the motion (e.g. motion model):
    - *"Given what I knew before, where do I expect the vehicle to be now?"*

  - **Measurement**: use the knowledge given by the sensor (e.g. GNSS measurements, Wi-Fi \acr{RTT} ranges, ...):
    -  *"The sensor says the vehicle is here."*


#### Kalman filter: main components

- Kalman filter delivers two important quantities:

  - $\hat{\mathbf{x}}_k$: the **state estimate**, the parameters we want to estimate (e.g. position, velocity, receiver clock,...)
  - $\mathbf{P}_k$: the **covariance matrix**, the uncertainty of the state estimate

- The main inputs to the filter are:

  - $z_k$: **measurement** at each epoch, affected by noise
  - $\mathbf{R}$: **measurement-noise covariance**, capturing the uncertainty of the measurements
  - $\mathbf{F}$: **motion model** predicts the next state
  - $\mathbf{Q}$: **process noise** captures the uncertainty of the motion model
  - $\mathbf{H}$: **measurement model** relates the state to the measurements (i.e. the design matrix)

#### Kalman filter: The processing loop

A better estimation is done by combining the **prediction** and **measurement** in a loop:

![source [Petteri Aimonen/Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalman_filter)](assets/figures/Basic_concept_of_Kalman_filtering.svg)

This loop runs continuously as new measurements arrive.


#### Kalman filter: Prediction

- *"What should the next state be, given the current state?"*
- This is done by propagating the state through the motion model ($\mathbf{F}$)

$$
\small
\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k|k-1} = \mathbf{F} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k-1|k-1}
$$

- The uncertainty of the prediction is also propagated through the motion model. We also add at this stage the **process noise** ($\mathbf{Q}$) to account for the uncertainty of the motion model:

$$
\small
\mathbf{P}_{k|k-1} = \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{P}_{k-1|k-1} \cdot \mathbf{F}^T + \mathbf{Q} \quad \left\{ \begin{eqnarray}
\mathbf{Q}\downarrow \quad &\Rightarrow & \color{green}{reliable\ model} \\
\mathbf{Q}\uparrow \quad &\Rightarrow &\color{red}{unreliable\ model} \\
\end{eqnarray} \right.
$$


#### Kalman filter: measurement model

- *"What does the sensor measure, given the current state?"*
  - Transfers the predicted state into the measurement space

- Therefore, for a nonlinear measurement model, the predicted measurement ($\hat{\mathbf{z}}_{k|k-1}$) is computed as:

$$
\hat{\mathbf{z}}_{k|k-1} = h\left(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k|k-1}\right)
$$

- The matrix $\mathbf{H}_k$ is the Jacobian of $h$ evaluated at the predicted state:

$$
\mathbf{H}_k = \left.\frac{\partial h}{\partial \mathbf{x}}\right|_{\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k|k-1}}
$$

- This is required for the **measurement update** step, where we compare the predicted measurement with the actual measurement.

#### Kalman filter: measurement noise

- *"How should I update my prediction, given the new measurement?"*

- Since sensors are also uncertain, a measurement-noise covariance ($\mathbf{R}$) is introduced.

$$
\left\{ \begin{eqnarray}
\mathbf{R}\downarrow \quad &\Rightarrow & \color{green}{reliable\ measurement} \\
\mathbf{R}\uparrow \quad &\Rightarrow &\color{red}{unreliable\ measurement} \\
\end{eqnarray} \right.
$$

- Example: For GNSS measurements, $\mathbf{R}$ is usually diagonal, with entries $\sigma_{UERE,i}^2$.

#### Kalman filter: the two forces

- There are two types of uncertainty in the Kalman filter:

  1. Model uncertainty ($\mathbf{Q}$)
  2. Measurement uncertainty ($\mathbf{R}$)

- Then the question is: *How much should I move my estimate?*

  - If $\mathbf{R} \downarrow \quad \Rightarrow$ move strongly toward the measurement.
  - If $\mathbf{Q} \downarrow \quad \Rightarrow$ stay closer to the prediction.

- The "*how much*" is determined by the **innovation** (or residual, $\mathbf{y}_k$), weighted by the **Kalman gain** ($\mathbf{K}$)

#### Kalman filter: innovation

- The **innovation** (or residual) is the difference between:
  - what the sensor measured, and
  - what our model predicted

$$
\underbrace{\mathbf{y}_k}_{innovation} =
\underbrace{\mathbf{z}_k}_{measurement} -
\underbrace{h\left(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k|k-1}\right)}_{prediction}
$$


If prediction and measurement agree:

$$
\mathbf{y}_k \approx 0
$$

and therefore there is little to correct.


#### Kalman filter: Kalman gain

The weighting of the innovation is the Kalman gain, defined as:

$$
\mathbf{K}_k = \mathbf{P}_{k|k-1} \cdot \mathbf{H}_k^T \ \left( \mathbf{H}_k \cdot \mathbf{P}_{k|k-1} \cdot \mathbf{H}_k^T + \mathbf{R} \right)^{-1}
$$

Intuition: *$\mathbf{K}$ determines how strongly the measurement should influence the prediction.*

$$
\begin{eqnarray}
\mathbf{K}\uparrow \quad &\Rightarrow& \text{trust the measurement more} \\
\mathbf{K}\downarrow \quad &\Rightarrow& \text{trust the prediction more}
\end{eqnarray}
$$


#### Kalman filter: measurement update

- Putting all the pieces together, the new state estimate is computed in the measurement update phase as:

$$
\underbrace{\hat{\mathbf{x}}_k}_{\text{new estimate}} =
\underbrace{\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k|k-1}}_{\text{prediction}}
+
\underbrace{ \underbrace{\mathbf{K}_k}_{\text{how much}} \cdot
\underbrace{\left(
\mathbf{z}_k -
h\left(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k|k-1}\right)
\right)}_{\text{how wrong}}}_{\text{correction}}
$$



- And the new uncertainty is updated as:

$$
\mathbf{P}_k = (\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{K}_k \cdot \mathbf{H}_k) \cdot \mathbf{P}_{k|k-1}
$$


#### Kalman filter: Kalman gain intuition

[Let's suppose we have a **1D position** problem, where the state and measurement are the position of a vehicle (e.g. $H = 1$). In this case, the Kalman gain is a scalar:]{style="font-size: 0.7em;"}

$$
\small
k_k =
\frac{p_{k|k-1}}{p_{k|k-1} + r}
$$

::: {.columns}

::: {.column}
[Measurement uncertain]{style="font-size: 0.6em; text-align: center;"}

$$
\tiny
\begin{eqnarray}
p_{k|k-1} = 1; \quad r = 9 \\
k_{k} = \frac{1}{1+9} = 0.1
\end{eqnarray}
$$

[Take only $10\%$ of the innovation (stay close to the prediction)]{style="font-size: 0.6em;"}
:::

::: {.column}
[Accurate measurement]{style="font-size: 0.6em; text-align: center;"}

$$
\tiny
\begin{eqnarray}
p_{k|k-1} = 9; \quad r = 1 \\
k_{k} = \frac{9}{9+1} = 0.9
\end{eqnarray}
$$

[Take $90\%$ of the innovation (stay close to the measurement)]{style="font-size: 0.6em;"}
:::

:::



#### Kalman filter: wrap-up

Putting all the pieces together:

![](assets/figures/kalman.svg)

#### Kalman example: one-dimensional position

- Goal: track a vehicle moving one-dimensionally at constant velocity.
- State (estimates): position and velocity $x_k = (p_k, v_k)$
- Measurements: noisy positions: $z_k = p_k + \varepsilon_k$

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: true
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

np.random.seed(4)

t = np.arange(20)
true_position = 2*t
measurement = true_position + np.random.normal(0, 3, len(t))

plt.figure(figsize=(10,3))
plt.plot(t, true_position, label="True position ($p_k$)")
plt.scatter(t, measurement, label="Measurements ($z_k$)")
plt.xlabel("Time")
plt.ylabel("Position (m)")
plt.legend()
plt.grid(alpha=.2)
plt.xticks(t)
plt.ylim(-5, 45)
plt.show()
```

- The measurements contain useful information — but they jump around.

#### Kalman example: measurement model


::: {.columns}

::: {.column}
[Measurement model ($\mathbf{H}$): *Which part of the state does this sensor observe?*]{style="font-size: 0.7em;"}
$$
\small
\mathbf{H}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0
\end{bmatrix}
$$
:::

::: {.column}
[Measurement noise ($\mathbf{R}$). Example: each epoch the sensor (e.g. GNSS receiver) gives us just one position measurement ($z_1$) with error $\sigma_{GNSS,1} = 3\ m$]{style="font-size: 0.7em;"}

$$
\small
\mathbf{R} = \begin{bmatrix}
3^2 \\
\end{bmatrix}
$$
:::

:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: true
sigma_gnss = 5

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 3))
plt.plot(t, true_position, label="True position ($p_k$)")
plt.errorbar(
  t,
  measurement,
  yerr=sigma_gnss,
  fmt="o",
  capsize=3,
  label="Measurements ($z_k$) ± 5 m",
)
plt.xlabel("Time")
plt.ylabel("Position (m)")
plt.legend()
plt.grid(alpha=.2)
plt.xticks(t)
plt.ylim(-5, 45)
plt.show()
```

#### Kalman example: propagation model


- Propagation (prediction) model ($\mathbf{F}$): *Prediction before using the new measurement.*

$$
\mathbf{F} =
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & \Delta t\\
0 & 1
\end{bmatrix}
$$

- Propagation noise ($\mathbf{Q}$), *How certain are you about the motion model?*
  - The $\mathbf{Q}$ is usually diagonal, with one entry for each state variable
  - For example, a $\sigma_p$ and $\sigma_v$ of $3\ m$ and $3\ m/s$ respectively would give:

$$
\mathbf{Q} =
\begin{bmatrix}
3^2 & 0\\
0 & 3^2
\end{bmatrix}
$$

#### Kalman example: running the filter

```{python}
from pygnss import filter
from pygnss.filter.ekf import Ekf

class ConstantVelocityModel(filter.Model):
  def __init__(self, dt):
    self.Phi = np.array([[1, dt], [0, 1]], dtype=float)

  def propagate_state(self, state):
    return self.Phi @ state

  def to_observations(self, state, compute_jacobian=False, **kwargs):
    H = np.array([[1, 0]], dtype=float) if compute_jacobian else None
    return filter.ModelObs(np.array([state[0]]), H)


class StateCollector(filter.StateHandler):
  def __init__(self):
    self.states = []
    self.covariances = []

  def process_state(self, state, covariance_matrix, **kwargs):
    self.states.append(state.copy())
    self.covariances.append(covariance_matrix.copy())


def run_filter(sigma_prediction, sigma_gnss):
  model = ConstantVelocityModel(dt=1)
  collector = StateCollector()
  kalman_filter = Ekf(
    x0=np.array([measurement[0], 0.0]),
    P0=np.zeros((2, 2)),
    Q=np.diag([sigma_prediction**2, sigma_prediction**2]),
    model=model,
    state_handler=collector,
  )

  for position_measurement in measurement:
    kalman_filter.process(
      np.array([position_measurement]),
      np.array([[sigma_gnss**2]]),
    )

  states = np.asarray(collector.states)
  covariances = np.asarray(collector.covariances)
  return states[:, 0], np.sqrt(covariances[:, 0, 0])


filter_cases = [
  ("Trust prediction", 1, 3, 0.1),
  ("Trust measurement", 3, 1, 0.9),
]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(10, 5), sharex=True, sharey=True)
for axis, (case_name, sigma_prediction, sigma_gnss, initial_gain) in zip(axes, filter_cases):
  estimated_position, estimated_sigma = run_filter(sigma_prediction, sigma_gnss)
  position_error = estimated_position - true_position
  error_bias = np.mean(position_error)
  error_std = np.std(position_error)
  error_rms = np.sqrt(np.mean(position_error**2))
  axis.plot(t, true_position, color="black", label="True position")
  axis.errorbar(
    t,
    measurement,
    yerr=sigma_gnss,
    fmt="o",
    capsize=2,
    alpha=0.45,
    label="GNSS measurement",
  )
  axis.plot(t, estimated_position, color="tab:blue", label="Kalman estimate")
  axis.fill_between(
    t,
    estimated_position - 2 * estimated_sigma,
    estimated_position + 2 * estimated_sigma,
    color="tab:blue",
    alpha=0.15,
    label="Estimate ± 2σ",
  )
  axis.set_title(
    f"{case_name}: σ_prediction = {sigma_prediction} m, "
    f"σ_measurement = {sigma_gnss} m (initial K ≈ {initial_gain})"
  )
  axis.set_ylabel("Position (m)")
  axis.text(
    0.82,
    0.05,
    f"Bias = {error_bias:.2f} m\n"
    f"Std. dev. = {error_std:.2f} m\n"
    f"RMS = {error_rms:.2f} m",
    transform=axis.transAxes,
    va="bottom",
    bbox={"facecolor": "white", "alpha": 0.8, "edgecolor": "none"},
  )
  axis.grid(alpha=.2)

axes[-1].set_xlabel("Time")
axes[-1].set_xticks(t)
axes[0].legend(ncol=4, fontsize="small")
axes[0].set_ylim(-10, 50)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```


::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-warning title="Kalman filter tuning"}
[Choosing the right values for $\mathbf{Q}$ and $\mathbf{R}$ is a key step to optimize a Kalman filter!]{style="font-size: 0.7em;"}
:::
:::


### PPP: key idea

::: {style="text-align: center;"}
[*Can we improve the meter-level accuracy of \acr{SPP}?*]{style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
:::

- Main error sources of \acr{SPP}:
  - **satellite orbit and clock errors** (broadcast information)
  - **ionosphere and troposphere** (atmospheric delays)

- Bonus points:
  - Can we use **carrier-phase measurements** to benefit from their higher precision? Caveat: they are ambiguous!

::: {style="text-align: center;"}
[The \acr{PPP} technique addresses these issues to achieve decimenter-level accuracy]{style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
:::

### PPP: main points

- The \acr{PPP} technique:
  - uses **precise satellite orbit and clock information** (instead of broadcast information).
  - uses **carrier-phase measurements** (instead of only code measurements)
  - uses a [**Kalman filter**](#kalman-filter-key-idea) with the knowledge of the receiver motion to smooth/improve the solution
  - adds additional estimated states to the Kalman filter (e.g. troposphere, ionosphere, etc.)
  - it may also use **ambiguity resolution** to unlock centimeter-level accuracy (implementation dependent)
- Main drawback:
  - requires a **long convergence time** to achieve decimeter-level accuracy.

::: {style="text-align: center;"}
[\acr{PPP} uses a **richer observation model** to increase accuracy]{style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
:::


### PPP: observation model

- Recall the [pseudorange](#measurement-model-pseudorange) and [carrier-phase](#measurement-model-carrier-phase) measurement models as well as the [range error budget](#uere-error-budget).

| Error source | Mitigation within \acr{PPP} |
|:---------------|:--------------------------|
| Orbit errors   | Precise orbits |
| Satellite clock errors | Precise clocks |
| Ionospheric error  | [Ionosphere-free combination](#iono-free-combination-definition) |
| Tropospheric error | additional unknown |
| Receiver noise and local effects | [**Kalman filter**](#kalman-filter-key-idea) |
| Code noise | Usage of carrier-phase + ambiguity resolution |


<!-- TODO make two plots, one for orbit error and another one for clock error -->

<!-- TODO make a plot with the position difference between SPP, PPP and RTK, use RTKLIB for this. Convergence time should be apparente -->

### PPP: larger state

- The estimation state for \acr{PPP} has more unknowns than \acr{SPP}. For example, an ionosphere-free PPP state can be written as:

$$
\small
\mathbf{x} =
\left [
  \underbrace{
\Delta x_{u,k} \quad
\Delta y_{u,k} \quad
\Delta z_{u,k} \quad
c \cdot \delta t_{u,k}
  }_{SPP} \quad
T_{z,\mathrm{wet}} \quad
N_1 \quad
N_2 \quad
\dots \quad
N_n \quad
\right]
$$


### PPP: navigation equations

- Below is a summary of the *partials* (i.e. coefficients) that are required to solve for a PPP state using code and phase [ionosphere-free measurements](#iono-free-combination-definition):
$$
\tiny
\begin{array}{c|ccccc|c}
 & x & y & z & c\,\delta t_u & T_{z,\mathrm{wet}} & N_i \\[1mm]
\hline
PR_{i, PC}
&
g_{x,i} & g_{y,i} & g_{z,i} & 1 & m_{w,i} & 0 \\[1mm]
L_{i, PC}
&
g_{x,i} & g_{y,i} & g_{z,i} & 1 & m_{w,i} & 1
\end{array}
$$


[where the geometric *partials* $g_{x,i}, g_{y,i}, g_{z,i}$ are the same as in \acr{SPP}:]{style="font-size: 0.7em;"}

$$
\tiny
g_{x,i} = -\frac{x_i-x_u}{\rho_i}, \quad
g_{y,i} = -\frac{y_i-y_u}{\rho_i}, \quad
g_{z,i} = -\frac{z_i-z_u}{\rho_i}
$$

- Note that the carrier phase introduces an additional unknown (the **integer ambiguity** $N_i$) for each satellite $i$.

### PPP: navigation solution

- Then the full linearized system for 4 satellites can be written as:

$$
\tiny
\underbrace{
\begin{bmatrix}
PR_{1,PC}-\rho_{1,0}\\
L_{1,PC}-\rho_{1,0}\\
PR_{2,PC}-\rho_{2,0}\\
L_{2,PC}-\rho_{2,0}\\
PR_{3,PC}-\rho_{3,0}\\
L_{3,PC}-\rho_{3,0}\\
PR_{4,PC}-\rho_{4,0}\\
L_{4,PC}-\rho_{4,0}
\end{bmatrix}
}_{\mathbf{y}\;\mathrm{(prefit\ residuals)}}
=
\underbrace{
\begin{bmatrix}
g_{x,1} & g_{y,1} & g_{z,1} & 1 & m_{w,1} & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\\
g_{x,1} & g_{y,1} & g_{z,1} & 1 & m_{w,1} & 1 & 0 & 0 & 0\\
g_{x,2} & g_{y,2} & g_{z,2} & 1 & m_{w,2} & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\\
g_{x,2} & g_{y,2} & g_{z,2} & 1 & m_{w,2} & 0 & 1 & 0 & 0\\
g_{x,3} & g_{y,3} & g_{z,3} & 1 & m_{w,3} & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\\
g_{x,3} & g_{y,3} & g_{z,3} & 1 & m_{w,3} & 0 & 0 & 1 & 0\\
g_{x,4} & g_{y,4} & g_{z,4} & 1 & m_{w,4} & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\\
g_{x,4} & g_{y,4} & g_{z,4} & 1 & m_{w,4} & 0 & 0 & 0 & 1
\end{bmatrix}
}_{\mathbf{H}_k\;\mathrm{(design\ matrix)}}
\cdot
\underbrace{
\begin{bmatrix}
\Delta x\\
\Delta y\\
\Delta z\\
c\,\delta t_u\\
\Delta T_{z,\mathrm{wet}}\\
N_1\\
N_2\\
N_3\\
N_4
\end{bmatrix}
}_{\Delta\mathbf{x}_{PPP}}
$$

### PPP: long convergence time

- The **long convergence time** of \acr{PPP} is due several factors:
  - additional unknowns for the integer ambiguities $N_i$
  - correlation between the wet troposphere, clock and the integer ambiguities
- Longer geoemtry diversity (i.e. more satellites) helps to reduce the convergence time.
  - This decorrelates the different unknowns of the filter


### PPP: precise products

- The precise products are provided by several organizations, such as the [International GNSS Service (IGS)](https://www.igs.org/). These products cover:
  - **precise satellite orbits** (in ITRF)
  - **precise satellite clocks** (in GPS time)
- The products are available in different formats, such as:
  - **SP3**: for precise orbits
  - **CLK**: for precise clocks
- Accurate ionospheric models are also available, such as the [\acr{GIM}](#ionosphere-error-daily-variation)
  - These are needed to shorten the convergence time of PPP (specially for ambiguity resolution) in algorithms such as Fast PPP (see [@rovira2016fast])
  - Delivered also by \acr{SBAS}

### Differential techniques

::: {style="text-align: center;"}
*How to exploit the fact that the larger error sources in GNSS are highly correlated?*
:::

- This applies specially to:
  - Atmospheric errors (ionosphere and troposphere)
  - Satellite orbit and clock errors
- What if we could use a **reference station** (aka **base station**) at a known location and change the measurement model so these errors are eliminated?


### Differential techniques: base station

![](assets/figures/differential_positioning.svg)


### Differential techniques: OSR

- \acr{OSR}.

- **Base station $\rightarrow$ rover:** GNSS observations
  - Code $PR$
  - Carrier phase $\phi$
  - Doppler
- Corrections are **implicit** through the reference observations

- Typical techniques:
  - \acr{DGNSS}.
  - \acr{RTK}.
  - \acr{NRTK} / \acr{VRS}

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal" title="In OSR, Base transmits observations; the rover forms the differences"}
:::

### Differential techniques: SSR

- \acr{SSR}.

- **Correction service $\rightarrow$ rover:** estimates of GNSS error states
- Corrections are provided **per satellite / signal**, such as:
  - Satellite orbit corrections
  - Satellite clock corrections
  - Code and phase biases
  - Atmospheric corrections, when provided

- Typical techniques:
  - \acr{PPP}.
  - \acr{PPP-RTK}.


::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal" title="In SSR, Base transmits corrections; the rover corrects raw observations"}
:::


### Differential techniques: OSR vs SSR

| | **OSR** | **SSR** |
|---|---|---|
| Transmitted | Observations | Error states / corrections |
| Reference | Base station(s) | Correction service |
| Rover model | Differenced | Undifferenced (raw) |
| Typical solution | RTK / NRTK | PPP / PPP-RTK |
| Coverage | Regional | Regional / global |
| Main concept | **Cancel errors by differencing** | **Model & correct errors** |

In summary:

$$
\boxed{\text{OSR: measurements}}
\qquad
\boxed{\text{SSR: corrections}}
$$


### Code-based Differential GNSS

- From the [pseudorange measurement model](#measurement-model-pseudorange), the **single-difference** between the rover ($r$) and the base station ($b$), observing the same satellite and signal, is:

$$
\begin{eqnarray}
\Delta PR_{r,b}^i &=& PR_r^i - PR_b^i \\
      &=& \Delta \rho_{r,b}^i + c \cdot \Delta \delta t_{r,b} + \Delta I_{r,b}^i + \Delta T_{r,b}^i + \Delta K_{r,b,s} + \Delta \varepsilon_{r,b}^i
\end{eqnarray}
$$

- Since the same satellite and signal are observed at both receivers:
  - The satellite clock error ($c\cdot \delta t^i$) and satellite-dependent bias cancel exactly.
  - The receiver code-bias difference ($\Delta K_{r,b,s}=K_{r,s}-K_{b,s}$) remains.
  - For a short baseline, the atmospheric differences ($\Delta I_{r,b}^i$ and $\Delta T_{r,b}^i$) are small, but do not generally vanish.
  - For independent, equal-variance receiver noise, $\sigma_{\Delta\varepsilon}=\sqrt{2}\,\sigma_{\varepsilon}$.


#### Code-based Differential GNSS: solution

- Define the baseline from the base station to the rover as $\mathbf{b_{rb}}=\mathbf{p}_r-\mathbf{p}_b$.
  - The solver estimates a correction to an a-priori baseline: $\mathbf{b_{rb}}=\mathbf{b_{rb,0}}+\Delta\mathbf{b_{rb}}$.
- The rover position is then computed as:
$$
\mathbf{p}_r = \mathbf{p}_b +  \mathbf{b_{rb}}
$$

- Let $\Delta\rho_{r,b}^i=\rho_r^i-\rho_b^i$ and define
  $\mathbf{g}_i=-\frac{\mathbf{s}_i-\mathbf{p}_{b,0}}{\rho_{b,0}^i}$, so that
  $\Delta\rho_{r,b}^i\approx\Delta\rho_{r,b,0}^i+\mathbf{g}_i^\mathsf{T}\Delta\mathbf{b}_{rb}$.

$$
\tiny
\begin{bmatrix}
\Delta PR_{r,b}^{1} - \Delta \rho_{r,b,0}^1\\
\Delta PR_{r,b}^{2} - \Delta \rho_{r,b,0}^2\\
\Delta PR_{r,b}^{3} - \Delta \rho_{r,b,0}^3\\
\Delta PR_{r,b}^{4} - \Delta \rho_{r,b,0}^4
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
g_{x,1} & g_{y,1} & g_{z,1} & 1\\
g_{x,2} & g_{y,2} & g_{z,2} & 1\\
g_{x,3} & g_{y,3} & g_{z,3} & 1\\
g_{x,4} & g_{y,4} & g_{z,4} & 1
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
\Delta b_x\\
\Delta b_y\\
\Delta b_z\\
c \Delta \delta t_{rb}
\end{bmatrix}
$$

#### Real Time Kinematics

- \acr{RTK} uses carrier-phase measurements from a known base station and a rover.
- As in \acr{DGNSS}, the rover estimates the baseline relative to the base station.
- Unlike code-based \acr{DGNSS}, \acr{RTK} also solves the integer ambiguities of the carrier-phase observations.

- For satellite $i$, the single difference between rover ($r$) and base ($b$) is:

$$
\tiny
\begin{eqnarray}
\Delta L_{r,b}^i &=& L_r^i - L_b^i \\
&=& \Delta\rho_{r,b}^i + c \cdot \Delta\delta t_{r,b}
 + \Delta I_{r,b}^i + \Delta T_{r,b}^i + \Delta k_{r,b}^i
 + \lambda \cdot \Delta N_{r,b}^i + \Delta\varepsilon_{r,b}^i
\end{eqnarray}
$$

  - Satellite clock errors and satellite-dependent biases cancel exactly.
  - The receiver clock difference and ambiguity difference remain.
  - For a short baseline, atmospheric differences are small

#### RTK: carrier-phase double difference

- A second difference between satellites $i$ and $j$ removes the receiver clock difference as well as the biases ($k$):

$$
\nabla\Delta L_{r,b}^{i,j} = \Delta L_{r,b}^i - \Delta L_{r,b}^j
$$

- The double-difference model is:

$$
\nabla\Delta L_{r,b}^{i,j} = \nabla\Delta\rho_{r,b}^{i,j} + \nabla\Delta I_{r,b}^{i,j} + \nabla\Delta T_{r,b}^{i,j} + \lambda \cdot \nabla\Delta N_{r,b}^{i,j} + \nabla\Delta\varepsilon_{r,b}^{i,j}
$$

- The double difference contains no receiver or satellite clock terms.
- $\nabla\Delta N_{r,b}^{i,j}$ is an **integer**, enabling integer ambiguity resolution.

#### RTK: positioning solution

- Define the baseline as $\mathbf{b}_{rb}=\mathbf{p}_r-\mathbf{p}_b$.
- Linearizing the double-difference geometric range around an a-priori baseline gives:

$$
\nabla\Delta\rho_{r,b}^{i,j} \simeq \nabla\Delta\rho_{r,b,0}^{i,j}
 + \mathbf{g}_{i,j}^{\mathsf{T}}\Delta\mathbf{b}_{rb}
$$

- The rover first estimates a **float solution** for the baseline and ambiguities.
- It then performs **integer ambiguity resolution** and recomputes the baseline with the fixed integers.
- Once fixed, the ambiguities enable centimeter-level positioning for short baselines.


#### RTK Network

- Single-base RTK is limited by the baseline length because atmospheric and orbit errors become less correlated with distance.
- \acr{NRTK} uses a network of reference stations to estimate spatially varying errors and provide corrections to the rover.
- The network can select a nearby reference station, form a network solution, or generate a \acr{VRS}.

#### RTK Virtual network

- A \acr{VRS} is generated near the rover from a network of real reference stations.
- The rover sends an approximate position to the correction service, usually through \acr{NTRIP}; the service returns observation-like corrections for the virtual station.
- The rover then applies the same carrier-phase differencing and integer ambiguity resolution as in single-base RTK.



### Differential techniques: RTCM format

<!-- TODO description of the RTCM format -->

- [RTCM](https://www.rtcm.org/rtcm-standards) is a standard format for differential GNSS messages. It is used to send corrections from a base station to a rover.

- It is a binary format that is compact and efficient for transmission.
- Widely used in the industry, and supported by many GNSS receivers and software.
- Usually sent via internet using the \acr{NTRIP} protocol

#### RTCM 3: message structure

RTCM 3 messages are **binary, variable-length frames**.

```
┌──────────┬──────────┬──────────────┬──────────────────────────┬──────────┐
│ Preamble │ Reserved │   Length     │       Data message       │   CRC    │
│  8 bits  │  6 bits  │   10 bits    │      0–1023 bytes        │ 24 bits  │
│   0xD3   │  000000  │ payload size │                          │ CRC-24Q  │
└──────────┴──────────┴──────────────┴──────────────────────────┴──────────┘
```

- **Preamble:** `0xD3` — synchronizes the receiver with the message
- **Reserved:** 6 bits
- **Length:** payload length in bytes
- **Data message:** contains the actual RTCM message
  - First **12 bits = Message Type (MT)**
  - Remaining bits depend on the message type
- **CRC-24Q:** detects transmission errors
- **Maximum payload:** 1023 bytes

#### RTCM 3: Main message types

RTCM messages provide **station information, observations, ephemerides and corrections**.

| Type | Message | Purpose |
|:---:|:---|:---|
| **1005 / 1006** | Reference station | Station coordinates / ARP |
| **107x** | GPS MSM | GPS multi-signal observations |
| **108x** | GLONASS MSM | GLONASS multi-signal observations |
| **109x** | Galileo MSM | Galileo multi-signal observations |
| **111x** | QZSS MSM | QZSS multi-signal observations |
| **112x** | BeiDou MSM | BeiDou multi-signal observations |
| **1019** | GPS ephemeris | GPS broadcast orbit & clock |
| **1045 / 1046** | Galileo ephemeris | Galileo broadcast orbit & clock |
| **1057–1062** | SSR | Satellite orbit / clock corrections |
| **1230** | GLONASS biases | GLONASS code / phase biases |

#### RTCM 3: MSM — Multiple Signal Messages

| Message Type | Satellite System |
|:------------:|:----------------:|
| `107x`         | GPS            |
| `108x`         | GLONASS        |
| `109x`         | Galileo        |
| `111x`         | QZSS           |
| `112x`         | BeiDou         |

The last digit `x` identifies the **MSM message level**:

| `x` | Description |
|:---:|:------------|
| 1,2,3   | Basic observations |
| 4,5   | Full observations |
| 6,7   | Higher-resolution observations |

- Examples:
  - `1074` = GPS MSM4
  - `1094` = Galileo MSM4
  - `1127` = BeiDou MSM7

## Positioning strategies

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR

    A(["Positioning<br/>strategies"]) --> B1(["Absolute<br/>positioning"])
    A --> B2(["Differential<br/>positioning"])

    B1 --> B11(["Code<br/>positioning"]) --> B111["Single Point Positioning<br/>SPP"]
    B1 --> B12(["Carrier-phase<br/>positioning"]) --> B121["Precise Point Positioning<br/>PPP"]

    B2 --> B21(["Code<br/>positioning"]) --> B211["Differential<br/>GNSS"] --> B2111["GBAS"]
    B211 --> B2112["SBAS"]

    B221 --> B2212["Network RTK"]

    classDef root fill:#172a3a,stroke:#172a3a,color:#ffffff,stroke-width:2px
```
